name: English for the Workplace (ESL)
objectives: In a job interview, answer common interview questions such as "Tell me about yourself" with short prepared answers, in 2 to 4 clear sentences each, with one real example from your work or life
Given common workplace safety words, signs and warnings, say what each one means and what to do, and report a hazard or injury to a supervisor, getting at least 4 of 5 right and reporting right away
When you get an instruction you do not fully understand, ask a supervisor or coworker for help and repeat the instruction back to check it, before you start the task

Given a work schedule or a change in your plans, read your shift times and tell your supervisor you will be late, are sick or need time off, saying the day, the time and the reason, as early as you can
When a customer comes to you, greet the customer, offer help and get another worker when you cannot help, politely and without guessing an answer

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting the job and staying safe

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The job interview: answering common questions
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Answer three common interview questions with short prepared answers.
This lesson builds toward: In a job interview, you will answer common interview questions such as "Tell me about yourself" with short prepared answers, in 2 to 4 clear sentences each, with one real example from your work or life.
Most interviews start with the same few questions. You can prepare your answers and practice them out loud. Short, clear answers are better than long ones.
"Tell me about yourself." Answer with your work, not your private life: "I have three years of experience in a restaurant kitchen. I am fast and careful. I want to grow in food service." "Why do you want this job?" Answer: "I like working with my hands, and this company has good training." "When can you start?" Answer: "I can start next Monday."
Other common questions: "What are your strengths?" ("I am on time and I learn fast.") "Can you work weekends?" ("Yes, I can work Saturdays.") At the end they often ask "Do you have any questions?" Have one ready: "What does a normal day look like?" or "What are the hours?"
Experience from your home country counts. Say it: "In Mexico I built houses for five years." If you did not understand a question, use the phrases you know: "Sorry, can you repeat the question, please?"
Step by step:
- Write short answers to the common questions.
- Use one real example from your work or life in each.
- Practice out loud until you can say them without reading.
- Prepare one question to ask at the end.
- If you miss a question, ask them to repeat it.
Words to know:
- "Experience": work you have done before.
- "Strengths": things you do well.
- "Interview": a meeting where an employer asks you questions to decide whether to hire you.
Official sources:
- USA Learns: free English courses for adults (Sacramento County Office of Education)
Try it now: Write your answers to "Tell me about yourself", "Why do you want this job?" and "When can you start?" for a job you want. Keep each to 2 to 4 sentences. Read them out loud three times, then ask a partner to interview you, or record yourself answering.
You can now answer common interview questions with short prepared answers, and ask a question at the end of an interview.

check.q: The interviewer says "Tell me about yourself." What is the best answer?
options: "I have two years of experience cleaning offices. I am careful and on time."
"I have three children and I like soccer and my favorite food is rice."
check.why: It talks about work and strengths in short, clear sentences.

check.q: The interviewer asks "Do you have any questions?" What is a good answer?
options: "What does a normal day look like?"
check.why: A question about the job shows you are interested.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Safety words, signs and warnings
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Say what common safety signs and warnings mean and what to do.
This lesson builds toward: Given common workplace safety words, signs and warnings, you will say what each one means and what to do, and report a hazard or injury to a supervisor, getting at least 4 of 5 right and reporting right away.
Safety words are the most important English at work. Learn them first. Signs: "Danger" means a serious hazard that can kill or badly hurt you. "Caution" or "Warning" means be careful. "Exit" is the way out. "Authorized personnel only" means only workers with permission can go in. "Wet floor" means it is slippery.
Spoken warnings are short and loud: "Watch out!" "Stop!" "Look out!" "Heads up!" (something may fall or come toward you). When you hear one, stop, look and move away from the danger.
Protective equipment words: "Wear your gloves." "Put on your safety glasses." "Hard hat" (a strong helmet). "Safety vest" (a bright vest so drivers see you). "Ear plugs". Your employer trains you on the equipment for your job. If you do not understand the training, ask.
Example conversation. Supervisor: "Heads up! Forklift coming." Worker: "Okay!" (steps back). Supervisor: "Always wear your vest in this area." Worker: "Yes. My vest, always in this area."
Words to know:
- "Hazard": something that can hurt you, like a wet floor or a moving machine.
- "Danger": a sign word for a serious hazard that can kill or badly hurt you.
- "Caution": a sign word that means be careful.
- "Protective equipment": gear that keeps you safe, like gloves, safety glasses or a hard hat.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Workers' rights (US Department of Labor)
Try it now: Make a safety word card for the job you want: write five safety words or signs you will see there and what each means. Say each one out loud. Then ask a partner to call out warnings ("Watch out!" "Heads up!") while you show what you would do.
You can now say what common safety signs, warnings and protective equipment words mean, and what to do when you hear a warning.

check.q: A coworker shouts "Heads up!" What do you do?
options: Stop, look and move away from what is coming
Shout "Heads up" back and stay there
check.why: "Heads up!" means something may fall or come toward you.

check.q: A door has a sign: "Authorized personnel only". What does it mean?
options: Only workers with permission can go in
check.why: "Authorized personnel only" means you need permission to go in.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reporting a problem or an injury
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Report a hazard or an injury to your supervisor right away.
This lesson builds toward: Given common workplace safety words, signs and warnings, you will say what each one means and what to do, and report a hazard or injury to a supervisor, getting at least 4 of 5 right and reporting right away.
If you see something unsafe, tell your supervisor right away: "Excuse me, there is a problem. There is oil on the floor in aisle 4." "This machine is making a strange noise." "The ladder is broken."
If you get hurt, even a little, tell your supervisor the same day: "I hurt my hand. I cut it on a box." "I hurt my back when I lifted that." Say where and when: "It happened at 10 o'clock, at the loading dock." In an emergency, call 911.
In the United States, OSHA (the federal agency for work safety) says workers have rights, including safety training in a language they understand, reporting a work injury, and asking for an inspection of an unsafe workplace. The law says your employer cannot punish you for using these rights. Check osha.gov/workers for the details.
Example conversation. Worker: "Excuse me, I need to report something. I slipped and hurt my knee." Supervisor: "When did it happen?" Worker: "About ten minutes ago, near the freezer." Supervisor: "Okay, let's fill out a report."
Step by step:
- Say "Excuse me, I need to report something."
- Say what is wrong: the hazard or the injury.
- Say where and when it happened.
- Report an injury the same day, even a small one.
- In an emergency, call 911.
Words to know:
- "Report": tell the right person about a problem.
- "Injury": harm to your body, like a cut, burn or hurt back.
- "Supervisor": the person in charge of your work.
- OSHA: the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the US federal agency for workplace safety.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Workers' rights (US Department of Labor)
Try it now: Practice only: write two short reports, one about a hazard (for example a wet floor) and one about a small made-up injury. Each one says what, where and when. Say them out loud as if you are talking to your supervisor.
You can now report a hazard or an injury to your supervisor, saying what, where and when, and name your basic safety rights.

check.q: You see a broken ladder at work. What do you say to your supervisor?
options: Nothing; someone else will see it
"Excuse me, the ladder in the back room is broken."
check.why: Telling your supervisor what and where lets them fix the hazard before someone is hurt.

check.q: You cut your finger a little at work. When do you report it?
check.why: Report every work injury the same day, even a small one.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Asking for help and checking instructions
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask for help and repeat an instruction back before you start.
This lesson builds toward: When you get an instruction you do not fully understand, you will ask a supervisor or coworker for help and repeat the instruction back to check it, before you start the task.
At work, a mistake can cost time, money or safety. It is always better to ask than to guess. Good workers ask questions.
To ask for help: "Excuse me, can you help me?" "Can you show me how to do this?" "Where do I put these boxes?" "What should I do next?" If you did not understand: "Sorry, can you explain that again, more slowly?"
Before you start, repeat the instruction back: "So, first I clean the tables, then I fill the napkins?" or "Okay, I put the blue boxes on shelf 3. Is that right?" Your supervisor will say "Yes" or fix it.
Example conversation. Supervisor: "Please restock aisle 7 and then break down the empty boxes." Worker: "Okay. So, first I restock aisle 7, then I break down the boxes. Where do the boxes go?" Supervisor: "In the recycling by the back door." Worker: "Got it. Thank you."
Step by step:
- Listen to the whole instruction.
- Ask about anything you did not understand.
- Repeat the steps back: "So, first ..., then ...?"
- Wait for "Yes" before you start.
- Ask again if you get stuck: "What should I do next?"
Words to know:
- "Instruction": words that tell you how to do a task.
- "Show me": do it in front of me so I can see how.
- "Got it": a short way to say "I understand".
Try it now: Ask a partner or family member to give you a three-step instruction in English (for example how to make a sandwich or fold a shirt). Repeat it back with "So, first ..., then ...?" before you do it. Then switch roles.
You can now ask a supervisor or coworker for help, and repeat an instruction back to check it before you start.

check.q: Your supervisor gives a long instruction. What do you do before you start?
options: Start and hope it is right
Repeat the steps back to check
check.why: Repeating the steps back catches mistakes before you start.

check.q: You do not know how to use the new machine. What do you say?
options: "Can you show me how to do this?"
check.why: "Can you show me?" asks for help in a safe, clear way.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Schedules: shifts, being late, sick days and time off
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Read your shift times and tell your supervisor you will be late, are sick or need time off.
This lesson builds toward: Given a work schedule or a change in your plans, you will read your shift times and tell your supervisor you will be late, are sick or need time off, saying the day, the time and the reason, as early as you can.
A shift is the time you work, for example "Monday, 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m." "a.m." is morning (before 12 noon) and "p.m." is afternoon and night. Your schedule may also say "OFF" for days you do not work.
If you will be late, tell your supervisor before your shift: "Hi, this is Carlos. I'm sorry, my bus is late. I will be about 20 minutes late." If you are sick: "Hi, this is Carlos. I'm sick today and I can't come in. I'm sorry." Every employer has its own rules for calling in, so check your handbook or ask your supervisor how and when to tell them.
To ask for time off, ask early, in person or in writing: "Can I have Friday the 14th off? I have an appointment." To trade a shift with a coworker: "Can I switch shifts with Maria on Saturday?"
Example text message: "Hi Ms. Johnson, this is Carlos from the morning shift. I am sick today and cannot come in. I'm sorry. I will let you know about tomorrow."
Step by step:
- Read your schedule: the days, start times and end times.
- Late or sick: tell your supervisor before your shift.
- Say who you are, what is wrong and when you will come.
- Ask for time off early, and say the date.
- Follow your employer's rules for calling in.
Words to know:
- "Shift": the hours you work on one day.
- "Call in sick": tell your employer you are sick and cannot work.
- "Time off": days you ask not to work.
- "Switch shifts": trade work times with a coworker.
Try it now: Write two messages to a supervisor with a made-up name: one to say you will be 15 minutes late, and one to call in sick. Each says who you are, what is wrong and when you will come. Read them out loud as a phone call.
You can now read your shift times, and tell your supervisor clearly that you will be late, are sick or need time off.

check.q: Your schedule says "Tuesday 2 p.m. - 10 p.m." When do you start work?
check.why: "p.m." means afternoon or night, so 2 p.m. is 2 in the afternoon.

check.q: Your bus is late and you will miss the start of your shift. What do you do?
options: Tell your supervisor before your shift starts
check.why: Telling your supervisor early is respectful and helps them plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking to customers
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Greet a customer, offer help and get another worker when you cannot help.
This lesson builds toward: When a customer comes to you, you will greet the customer, offer help and get another worker when you cannot help, politely and without guessing an answer.
Customers like workers who are friendly and clear. Greet them: "Hi, welcome!" or "Good morning." Offer help: "Can I help you find something?" "What can I get for you?"
If you know the answer, keep it short: "Yes, it's in aisle 9." "It comes with fries." If you do not know, never guess. Say: "Let me check for you." or "One moment, please. I'll get my manager."
If the customer talks too fast: "Sorry, could you say that again, please?" If they are upset, stay calm and polite: "I'm sorry about that. Let me get someone who can help." End with: "Have a nice day!"
Example conversation. Worker: "Hi, welcome! Can I help you find something?" Customer: "Do you have this jacket in a large?" Worker: "Let me check for you. One moment, please." (checks) "Yes, here you go." Customer: "Thanks!" Worker: "You're welcome. Have a nice day!"
Step by step:
- Greet: "Hi, welcome!"
- Offer help: "Can I help you find something?"
- Answer short if you know.
- If you do not know: "Let me check for you." or get a manager.
- End: "Have a nice day!"
Words to know:
- "Customer": a person who buys or uses what a business sells.
- "Manager": a person who is in charge of a store or team.
- "Let me check": a polite way to say you will find the answer.
Try it now: Final task: write your Workplace English script for the job you want: your answer to "Tell me about yourself", two more interview answers, three safety words with their meanings, a call-in-sick or late message, and two phrases for a customer or for asking a coworker for help. Practice it out loud or in a role play, and record yourself if you can.
You can now greet a customer, offer help, and get the right person when you do not know the answer.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Interview answers Answers are missing, very long, or about private life instead of work. "Tell me about yourself" and two more answers, each 2 to 4 clear sentences with one real example. Says them out loud without reading and adds a question to ask at the end. Safety words Fewer than three words, or the meanings are wrong. Three safety words or signs for the job, each with the right meaning. Also shows how to report a hazard or injury: what, where and when. Asking for help No phrase for asking for help, or no way to check an instruction. One phrase to ask for help and one sentence that repeats an instruction back. Uses them correctly in a role play with a partner. Late or sick message Missing who you are, what is wrong or when you will come. A clear, polite message with name, reason and timing. Also notes how their employer wants call-ins (handbook or supervisor). Customer phrases No customer phrases, or the phrases are not polite. A greeting with an offer of help, and a phrase for when you do not know. Handles an upset customer politely in a role play. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, practice that part and try again.

check.q: A customer asks a question and you do not know the answer. What do you say?
check.why: Checking or getting a manager is polite and gives the customer the right answer.

check.q: A customer walks up to you. What is a good first thing to say?
options: "Hi, welcome! Can I help you find something?"
check.why: A greeting and an offer of help start the conversation well.
